historical_references.reference: Nowrooz is the Persian name for the first day of Farvardin, the first month in the Iranian calendar, which marks the beginning of the new year.
historical_references.time_period: The Iranian New Year has been celebrated for over 2,500 years.
historical_references.context: The origin of Nowrooz can be traced back to ancient Persian civilizations, particularly the Achaemenid Empire (550-330 BC) and the Sassanid Empire (224-651 AD). The festival was influenced by Zoroastrianism, the dominant religion during these empires, and was a time for purification, feasting, and renewal.

historical_references.reference: Nowrooz is also celebrated in other countries with significant Islamic populations, including Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Tajikistan.
historical_references.time_period: The spread of Islam throughout Central Asia during the medieval period led to the adoption of Nowrooz by Muslim communities in the region.
historical_references.context: Although Nowrooz has its roots in Persian and Zoroastrian traditions, it has been adapted by Islamic communities to include religious elements and symbolism. For example, the haft sin (seven S's) table spread on Nowrozz is believed to represent the seven heavens in Islamic cosmology.

modern_usage.modern_context: Nowrooz is the name of the Iranian New Year, which marks the first day of Farvardin, the first month of the Iranian Solar Hijri Calendar (March 20 or 21 in the Gregorian Calendar). It is a time for renewal and rebirth, celebrated with family gatherings, traditional foods, and the exchange of gifts. In modern times, the holiday has gained global popularity and is celebrated not only in Iran, but also in countries with large Iranian diaspora populations such as the United States, Canada, and Europe.
